$$ \omega=-i\gamma_{0}\pm\sqrt{\omega_{0}^{2}-\gamma_{0}^{2}}, $$

where

$$ \omega_{0}=k_{\parallel}v_{\mathrm{A}}\sqrt{\frac{1+k^{2}\rho_{\tau}^{2}}{1+k_{\parallel}^{2}d_{i}^{2}+k^{2}d_{e}^{2}}},\quad\gamma_{0}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\eta k^{2}}{1+k_{\parallel}^{2}d_{i}^{2}+k^{2}d_{e}^{2}}. $$

As it results from a fluid model, this dispersion relation is a poor approximation to reality in a number of important situations. For example, when both $k\rho_{\tau}\sim 1$ and $kd_{e}\sim 1$ , real AW undergo strong Landau damping, completely ignored in this model; even the real frequency in this regime also differs significantly from this two-fluid model[54]. For $k\rho_{s}\sim 1$ but $kd_{e}\ll 1$ and $k\rho_{i}\ll 1$ (fluid kinetic AW) and $kd_{e}\sim 1$ but $k\rho_{\tau}\ll 1$ (fluid inertial AW), the collisionless damping is relatively weak, and (142) is somewhat acceptable.

## Appendix B Reduced dispersive AW equations

Evidence suggests that the small-scale turbulence in the solar wind[55] consists of kinetic AW; in the aurora, both inertial and kinetic AW exist in different regions [56]. Modelling of this turbulent cascade is often done assuming that typical linear and nonlinear frequencies are small compared to $\Omega_{i}$ [31, 32, 30]. To make contact with these existing theories, we use the following ordering scheme. First, we write the magnetic field $b$ as

$$ \boldsymbol{b}=v_{\mathrm{A}}+\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}+\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}b_{z}, $$

where $v_{\mathrm{A}}$ is the mean Alfvén velocity and $\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}$ and $b_{z}$ are the (small-amplitude) magnetic fluctuations in velocity units in the perpendicular and $z$ directions. Similarly, we write

$$ n=1+\tilde{n}, $$

where $\tilde{n}$ is the normalized density fluctuation.

We assume that the perpendicular lengthscales of our fluctuations are small compared to their parallel lengthscales, and expand in $\epsilon\ll 1$ , defined via

$$ \frac{\partial_{z}}{\nabla_{\perp}}\sim\epsilon^{2}\ll 1. $$

We also assume that the linear timescales are Alfvénic, and comparable to the nonlinear timescales and the electron-ion collision frequency, i.e.

$$ \partial_{t}\sim v_{\mathrm{A}}\partial_{z}\sim\boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla_{\perp}\sim\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla_{\perp}\sim\nu_{ei}, $$

which implies that the fluctuation amplitudes are ordered as

$$ \frac{u_{\perp}}{v_{\mathrm{A}}}\sim\frac{b_{\perp}}{v_{\mathrm{A}}}\sim\epsilon^{2}\ll 1. $$

We also restrict ourselves to low $\beta$ and small mass ratio, taking

$$ \beta=\frac{c_{s}^{2}}{v_{\mathrm{A}}^{2}}\sim\frac{Zm_{e}}{m_{i}}\epsilon^{2}. $$

We wish to include the kinetic and inertial Alfvén dispersion, so we must order77 7 Again (cf. discussion in Appendix A), keeping both terms simultaneously is a poor approximation, but we will here do it anyway to compare with previous work.

$$ \rho_{\tau}\nabla_{\perp}\sim d_{e}\nabla_{\perp}\sim 1, $$

implying that the resistive term is also kept: since $\eta=\nu_{ei}d_{e}^{2}$ ,

$$ \eta\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\sim\partial_{t}. $$

Eq. (151) also means that $d_{i}$ is large compared to the perpendicular scales,

$$ d_{i}\nabla_{\perp}\sim\epsilon^{-1}, $$

but small compared to the parallel scales,

$$ d_{i}\partial_{z}\sim\epsilon, $$

a regime typical for auroral fluctuations and in some laboratory experiments. This also means that the typical timescales are small compared to $\Omega_{i}$ ,

$$ \frac{1}{\Omega_{i}}\partial_{t}\sim\epsilon. $$

We will assume from the outset (and show that this is consistent) that $b_{z}$ and $u_{z}$ are at least as small as the perpendicular fluctuations $\boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}$ ; we will deduce the ordering for $\tilde{n}$ from the equations, but assume it is small compared to unity. The $z$ -component of the induction equation (139) at lowest order yields

$$ \nabla_{\perp}\cdot\boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}=-\frac{1}{\Omega_{i}}\nabla_{\perp}\times\mathrm{d}_{t}\boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}\sim\epsilon^{2}\Omega_{i}, $$

meaning that the perpendicular velocity is only slightly compressive: its divergence is one order smaller than its curl. This can be inserted into the continuity equation (137), which then gives at lowest order

$$ \mathrm{d}_{t}\tilde{n}=\frac{1}{\Omega_{i}}\nabla_{\perp}\times\mathrm{d}_{t}\boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}, $$

from which

$$ \tilde{n}\sim\epsilon. $$

Turning now to the perpendicular momentum equation (138), at lowest order we just obtain the pressure balance

$$ c_{s}^{2}\tilde{n}=-b_{z}v_{\mathrm{A}}, $$

whence in fact, we see that

$$ \frac{b_{z}}{v_{\mathrm{A}}}\sim\epsilon^{3}. $$

The lowest order terms of the $z$ -component of the momentum equation (138) are

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}_{t}u_{z}= \displaystyle v_{\mathrm{A}}\partial_{z}b_{z}+\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla_{\perp}b_{z}+\frac{Zm_{e}}{m_{i}}d_{i}\mathrm{d}_{t}\nabla_{\perp}\times\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp} \displaystyle+d_{e}^{2}[\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}\times\nabla_{\perp}b_{z}]\cdot\nabla_{\perp}\nabla_{\perp}\times\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}, $$

from which we can deduce that88 8 We have used this to preemptively drop the term involving $u_{z}$ on the RHS of (138) when writing (161).

$$ \frac{u_{z}}{v_{\mathrm{A}}}\sim\epsilon^{3}. $$

At lowest order, the perpendicular induction equation reads

$$ \mathrm{d}_{t}\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}=v_{\mathrm{A}}\partial_{z}\boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}+\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla_{\perp}\boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}+d_{i}\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}\times\nabla_{\perp}\mathrm{d}_{t}u_{z}+\eta\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}, $$

into which we insert (161) to eliminate $u_{z}$ and (159) to eliminate $b_{z}$ in favor of $\tilde{n}$ , yielding

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}= \displaystyle v_{\mathrm{A}}\partial_{z}\boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}+\nabla_{\perp}\times(\boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}\times\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}) \displaystyle-\frac{c_{s}^{2}}{\Omega_{i}}\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}\times\nabla_{\perp}\left[v_{\mathrm{A}}\partial_{z}\tilde{n}+\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla_{\perp}\tilde{n}\right] \displaystyle-d_{e}^{2}\frac{c_{s}^{2}}{\Omega_{i}}\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}\times\nabla_{\perp}[\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}\times\nabla_{\perp}\tilde{n}\cdot\nabla_{\perp}\nabla_{\perp}\times\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}] \displaystyle+d_{e}^{2}\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}\times\nabla_{\perp}\mathrm{d}_{t}\nabla_{\perp}\times\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}+\eta\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}. $$

To make further progress, note that since (140) at lowest order is just $\nabla_{\perp}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}=0+O(\epsilon^{3})$ , we may write $\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}$ in terms of a flux function

$$ \boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}=\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}\times\nabla_{\perp}\psi. $$

Similarly, because $\nabla_{\perp}\cdot\boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}$ is small (cf. 156), at lowest order we can write the perpendicular velocity in terms of a stream function99 9 We have not completely neglected the compressive part of the velocity; it sets the density fluctuations via (156): in Secs. II and III, it plays a more active role in the dynamics and we must include it explicitly.

$$ \boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}=\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}\times\nabla_{\perp}\phi. $$

Nonlinear terms are expressed in terms of these scalar functions as

$$ \boldsymbol{u}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla_{\perp}f=\left\{\phi,f\right\},\quad\boldsymbol{b}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla_{\perp}f=\left\{\psi,f\right\} $$

where the Poisson bracket $\left\{f,g\right\}=\nabla_{\perp}f\times\nabla_{\perp}g$ . To lowest order,

$$ \mathrm{d}_{t}f=\partial_{t}f+\left\{\phi,f,.\right\} $$

Writing (157) in terms of $\phi$ results in

$$ \tilde{n}=\frac{1}{\Omega_{i}}\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\phi, $$

the density fluctuations are proportional to the vorticity of the flow. Writing (164) and the curl of the perpendicular momentum equation (138) in terms of $\phi$ and $\psi$ only, we obtain a closed set of nonlinear equations for the DAW,

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\phi+\{\phi,\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\phi\}= \displaystyle v_{\mathrm{A}}\partial_{z}\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\psi+\{\psi,\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\psi\}, \displaystyle\partial_{t}[\psi-d_{e}^{2}\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\psi]= \displaystyle v_{\mathrm{A}}\partial_{z}[\phi-\rho_{\tau}^{2}\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\phi] \displaystyle+\{\psi-d_{e}^{2}\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\psi,\phi-\rho_{\tau}^{2}\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\phi\} \displaystyle+\eta\nabla_{\perp}^{2}\psi. $$

These "reduced dispersive Alfvén wave" (RDAW) equations are identical to those used in Seyler & Xu (2003)[31] to study auroral fluctuations; however, those authors did not provide a systematic derivation1010 10 To the author’s knowledge, one does not appear in press.. The equations are also similar to the reduced gyrokinetic equations in Zocco & Schekochihin 2011[30] (a.k.a. "KREHM"): however, that model is significantly more sophisticated, incorporating a rigorous treatment of the ion and electron kinetics.

Here, we will just make two important points about the above equations. First, the Poisson brackets all vanish if gradients are all in one direction: so any one-dimensional configuration of fields is an exact solution; i.e., there is no one-dimensional wave steepening retained in this system. Second, if both $\rho_{\tau}\nabla_{\perp}\ll 1$ and $d_{e}\nabla_{\perp}\ll 1$ , the RVDAW equations become reduced magnetohydrodynamics (RMHD), for which $\phi=\pm\psi$ are exact nonlinear solutions, travelling in opposite directions along $\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}$ , regardless of three-dimensional structure. In this non-dispersive limit, non-trivial nonlinear interaction only occurs between counterpropagating waves. This is despite the density fluctuations (169) and despite $d_{i}\nabla_{\perp}\gg 1$ : to this order, the compressive nature of the wave makes no difference to the nonlinear dynamics. Upon including the dispersive effects, nonlinear interaction does occur between co-propagating waves (provided their perpendicular wavevectors also point in different directions) with different perpendicular scales, because smaller-scale waves "catch up" to larger-scale ones.
